Assessing Spatial Equity in Multimodal Accessibility to Cooling-Effective Urban Green Space: A Case Study of London Abstract

Assessing Spatial Equity in Multimodal Accessibility to Cooling-Effective Urban Green Space: A Case Study of London Chi Chin Christy Choi CASA0010, MSc Urban Spatial Science Supervisor: Dr Andrew MacLachlan Repository: https://github.com/christychoicc/london-cooling-access-equity.git This dissertation is submitted in part requirement for the MSc in the Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment, UCL Word count: 11,998 2026-10-25 Abstract Climate change and rapid urbanisation have contributed to the increasing frequency and intensity of extreme heat events, placing significant pressures on urban populations and raising environmental justice concerns. While urban green spaces (UGS) are important infrastructure for heat mitigation, current efforts remain limited in integrating UGS cooling performance with accessibility and environmental equity. To address this gap, we assess the extent to which multimodal accessibility to cooling-effective UGS is equitably distributed across heat exposed and socioeconomically deprived neighbourhoods in the case of London. Land surface temperature (LST) was used to screen UGS with cooling effects through a cumulative approach of park cooling indicators. Using the r5r package for R, travel time between each origin and potential destination was used to quantify cumulative opportunity accessibility to cooling-effective UGS by public transit, walking, and cycling reachable within 15- and 60-minute thresholds. Spatial relationships between accessibility, heat exposure and socioeconomic deprivation were assessed by Bayesian Hierarchical Besag-York-Mollié (BYM2) models implemented in the R-INLA package, complemented by Bivariate Local Indicator of Spatial Association (BiLISA). Applying this methodological approach to London, the findings reveal that only 32.77% of UGS ≥ 2ha were both cooling-effective and publicly accessible, with access to these spaces varying substantially by travel mode and time thresholds. Although higher heat exposure was generally associated with greater accessibility, such relationship weakens with increasing socioeconomic deprivation. Despite the overall pattern, inequity hotspots remained persistent at the local scale. Altogether, this study demonstrates an integrated data-driven approach for assessing spatial inequalities in cooling-effective UGS potential accessibility, enabling identification of local green spaces accessibility deficiencies and inform targeted green infrastructure and urban heat resilience planning strategies to address specific inequalities. Keywords: Urban heat; urban green space; accessibility; spatial inequality; environmental justice

Chapter 1 Introduction Extreme heat has emerged as one of the greatest challenges faced by cities around the world, driven by the intensification of rapid urbanisation and climate change. In response to these challenges, international policy frameworks such as the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the New Urban Agenda emphasised the need for sustainable, inclusive and equitable solutions (United Nations, 2015; UN Habitat, 2020). Rising temperatures and more frequent extreme heat events place increasing pressure on urban habitability, resilience, and public services (Mohajerani, Bakaric and Jeffrey-Bailey, 2017). Cities are particularly vulnerable to the rapid expansion of built-up environments, often replacing natural land surfaces with impervious, heat-absorbent materials. This alters local microclimates, accelerates urban overheating and intensifies the urban heat island (UHI) effect, whereby urban air and surface temperatures are significantly higher than those in surrounding rural or peri-urban environments (Kleerekoper, van Esch and Salcedo, 2012; Mohajerani, Bakaric and Jeffrey-Bailey, 2017). More importantly, the consequence of urban overheating extends beyond environmental concerns to social and public health impacts. Exposure to elevated temperatures is associated with a range of adverse physical and mental health outcomes such as thermoregulatory stress, heat fatigue, heat stroke, and increased fatalities (Kleerekoper, van Esch and Salcedo, 2012; Heaviside, Macintyre and Vardoulakis, 2017; Xu et al., 2022). Yet, such impacts are not limited to the most extreme heat events. For instance, in England, an additional 1,311 heat-associated fatalities were recorded during summer heat episodes in 2024 despite being the coolest summer since 2015 (GOV.UK, 2026). This suggests that even under comparably less extreme conditions, urban heat can still place serious pressures on public health. As unprecedented extreme heat events become more frequent, prolonged, and intense (World Health Organization, 2026), urban heat is recognised not only as an environmental issue, but also increasingly a public health concern. Urban green space (UGS) is widely recognised as a nature-based approach for mitigating urban heat and improving human health (Bowler et al., 2010a; Lin and Li, 2025). Urban vegetation can disrupt the thermal continuity of urban environments through shading, heat absorption, and evapotranspiration (Xu et al., 2022; Y. Li et al., 2024). Through the park cool island effect, UGS can reduce temperatures within green spaces and extend cooling benefits into surrounding areas, helping buffer heat stress under high temperatures (Shishegar, 2014; Dong et al., 2024). However, UGS does not provide same levels of cooling benefits. The cooling-effectiveness of UGS is heterogeneous, exhibiting spatial variation depending on factors such as size, vegetation density, shape, and spatial configuration (Wang and Ren, 2025). Consequently, spatial proximity to green space does not equate to access to thermal comfort. As cooling performance varies, the extent of its true benefits depends on reachability shaped by temporal, functional and normative factors such as travel time, mode, cost, and duration (Miller, 2018; Hassan et al., 2025). Despite growing recognition of UGS as a cooling infrastructure, both its distribution and cooling benefits remain uneven across neighbourhoods, particularly among lower socioeconomic and ethnic minority groups (Harlan et al., 2006; Li et al., 2026). Such inequalities demonstrate that urban heat mitigation is not only an environmental concern, but also a growing socio-spatial challenge. All things considered, green space provision reflects wider patterns of environmental injustice, and access to cooling relief is shaped by structural urban inequalities rather than by heat exposure alone (Wolch, Byrne and Newell, 2014). Taking London as a case study, the city has experienced severe and escalating heat events but remains unprepared for its consequences (Mayor of London, 2026b). Notably, London recorded 59 days above 30°C between 2014 and 2023, and 5 days above 35°C between 2019 and 2022 (IIED, n.d.). The Mayor of London (n.d.) noted that existing homes and buildings in London are not built for the warming climate, with projected impacts on health and social care systems set to increase. Many of those heat related fatalities are considered preventable, yet the London Climate Resilience Review argues that England is currently “ill-prepared” for heat risk with limited cooling opportunities, calling for urgent attention and action (Boyd, Leigh and Sutton, 2024). In response, the London Plan 2021 identifies urban green infrastructure as a key mechanism for addressing UHI, promoting health and wellbeing, and improving accessibility of open spaces (Mayor of London, 2021). Despite strong policy commitments, spatial evidence on whether London’s green infrastructure provides accessible cooling relief to neighbourhoods most exposed to heat and socioeconomic deprivation remains limited. By applying data driven insights across heat vulnerable areas, cooling-effectiveness, and multimodal accessibility, this allows for informing more equitable urban greening strategies. While existing literature shows the ability of UGS to mitigate urban heat and acknowledges its variation in cooling performance, few studies have integrated this into fields of cooling-effectiveness, accessibility, and environmental equity within one research framework. Consequently, based on existing research gaps, this study therefore aims to address 12 the research question of: To what extent is multimodal accessibility to cooling-effective urban green spaces equitably distributed across heat exposed and socioeconomically deprived areas in London? The specific objectives include: Through Earth observation indicators, which urban green space demonstrates cooling benefits, and which neighbourhoods experience greatest heat exposure in London? How accessible are cooling-effective green spaces across London’s neighbourhoods considering multi-modal transportation? To what extent do heat exposed and socioeconomically deprived neighbourhoods experience differentiated access to cooling-effective green spaces? This study is structured as follows. The first section lays out the background of this research. Section 2 provides a brief overview of the literature and policy on urban heat, UGS and accessibility. Section 3 describes the data and research methodology. The results are then presented in Section 4 following a discussion in Section 5, which also highlights policy implications and future research directions. Finally, Section 6 summarises and concludes the study.

Chapter 2 Literature Review As established in the introduction, urban heat is a growing environmental, public health and socio-spatial challenge. While UGS has been identified as a mitigation strategy, its benefits are unevenly distributed and may not be accessible to those most exposed or vulnerable. Building on this, this section is structured into four parts: the problem and policy context of urban heat (2.1), the role of UGS as a cooling infrastructure for mitigating urban heat (2.2), accessibility to cooling-effective UGS as an environmental justice (EJ) concern (2.3), and methodological approaches for studying cooling accessibility and spatial equity (2.4). 2.1 Urban Heat Problem Urban heat is one of the major climate risks faced by urban populations, widely recognised as an urban hazard resulting from the combined effects of climate change and urbanisation, with significant implications for urban sustainability and liveability (Mohajerani, Bakaric and Jeffrey-Bailey, 2017). As stated in the introduction, urban heat challenges wider global goals for sustainable and equitable development, as its impacts span beyond environmental concerns to public health and social inequality. Commonly conceptualised through the UHI effect, it reflects complex interactions between urban morphology, land cover and surface energy balance (Yeboah et al., 2025). The replacement of permeable surfaces with dense built materials (i.e. asphalt, concrete) increases heat absorption and storage while reducing evaporative cooling, thereby intensifying the UHI effect (Balany et al., 2020; Yeboah et al., 2025). However, urban heat is spatially uneven and varies significantly across the urban landscape (Moffett, Makido and Shandas, 2019). Variations in land surface materials, spatial distribution of buildings and building geometry can collectively influence local thermal conditions at the neighbourhood level (Kleerekoper, van Esch and Salcedo, 2012; Chen et al., 2016; Heaviside, Macintyre and Vardoulakis, 2017). In light of such intra-urban variation, urban heat should not be perceived as a spatially consistent phenomenon, but a spatially differentiated pattern of heat exposure. 2.1.1 Vulnerability of Cities to Urban Heat Building upon the intra-urban variation in urban heat, while land surface temperature (LST) can identify where thermal exposure is concentrated, it only provides a partial indication of urban heat, not fully explaining what populations are most at risk. (Karanja and Kiage, 2021; Niu et al., 2021). This is important as areas experiencing high temperatures do not necessarily correspond to areas of greater vulnerability. In this sense, urban heat is a socio-spatial problem, shaped by the interaction between physical heat exposure, social characteristics and sensitivity, building structure, housing density and access to resources (Brenkert and Malone, 2005; Wilhelmi and Hayden, 2010; Leal Filho et al., 2018; Karanja and Kiage, 2021; Li et al., 2022). Conceptually, literature emphasises that heat risk emerges through the intersection of hazard, exposure and vulnerability (Cardona et al., 2012). The IPCC (2001, p. 16) defines vulnerability as “degree to which a system is susceptible to or unable to cope with, adverse effects of climate change, including climate variability and extremes”, while Cutter (2006) specifies this as an individual potential for harm shaped by both spatial and non-spatial domains. Under this context, the impacts of high temperatures are mediated not only by where and when heat occurs, but also by who is exposed, who is more sensitive and who has the adaptive capacity to respond and cope (Kolokotroni and Giridharan, 2008; Karanja and Kiage, 2021; Li et al., 2022). The complexity of vulnerability is recognised in literature, often approached through topics of physiological sensitivity and wider societal conditions (Alonso and Renard, 2020). Physiological sensitivity refers to the physical risk factors that shape individuals’ response to heat. Extreme heat can exacerbate existing health conditions and increase heat-related hospitalisation, morbidity and mortality, especially during severe heatwave events (Heaviside, Macintyre and Vardoulakis, 2017). For instance, Hadei et al. (2024) found a 23% increase in heat-related mortality rate during heatwave events compared with normal days. This is particularly damaging for individuals with pre-existing physical and mental health conditions, older and younger populations, as these groups are more vulnerable due to reduced thermoregulation capacity and greater susceptibility to heat stress (Heaviside, Macintyre and Vardoulakis, 2017; Balany et al., 2020; Niu et al., 2021). Beyond physical exposure, the consequences of urban heat are also shaped by social vulnerability, with factors such as socioeconomic status, neighbourhood context, and access to resources influencing how individuals and communities are exposed to, manage and respond to heat (Niu et al., 2021). Mitchell and Chakraborty (2015) describe this as a “climate gap”, identifying significant associations between urban heat risk factors and lower socioeconomic status. Such inequalities may reflect prior planning, housing, and disinvestment practices that contributed to reduced green space provision, higher levels of heat exposure and limited access to cooling resources in marginalised communities (Xiao et al., 2023; Huang, Dombrowski and Stucky, 2025). Likewise, Niu et al. (2021) and Chen (2024) argue that heat disparities occur across certain population and income groups, who may face greater exposure to adverse heat impacts and lower adaptive capacity. In urban contexts, adaptive capacity is influenced by whether there is access to cooling resources. Studies have found that poorer neighbourhoods are disproportionately exposed to extreme heat and often have fewer physical and social resources (Harlan et al., 2006; Heaviside, Macintyre and Vardoulakis, 2017; Xie et al., 2026). Typically, higher surface temperatures are commonly associated with areas characterised by poverty, ethnic minority groups, lower educational attainment, older populations and higher crime rates (Heaviside, Macintyre and Vardoulakis, 2017), which may also have lower vegetation cover and reduced cooling capacity. Nevertheless, Alonso and Renard (2020) argue that physiological and socio-economic vulnerabilities vary spatially, with the former concentrating in urban centres and the latter in the periphery in Lyon. Specifically, socio-economic disadvantages and physiologically heat-sensitive populations do not necessarily concentrate in the same areas. This highlights that heat vulnerability should not be understood through physical proximity to heat, but through the interconnection between social, economic and biophysical conditions across multiple scales (Wilhelmi and Hayden, 2010). However, existing studies often measure heat vulnerability with different approaches, findings are not always comparable across different contexts. Therefore, addressing heat vulnerability requires a broader, context-specific socio-spatial approach that considers not only where heat occurs, but also whether communities can access the resources needed to cope. Such socio-spatial nature of urban heat vulnerability is particularly relevant in London, where heat exposure, housing conditions, and social disadvantage intersect unevenly across neighbourhoods. Characterised by dense urban form, London has extensive heat-retaining surfaces that intensify local thermal conditions and contribute to spatial clustering in heat vulnerability, with discernible heat-related health impacts (Wolf and McGregor, 2013). Zooming into neighbourhood-level, survey conducted during the August 2025 heatwave found lived experiences of urban heat are unevenly distributed, with Londoners in social housing and those facing economic disadvantage reporting more severe heat discomfort, having “fewer cooling measures” at home (Hewlett et al., 2026, p. 5). More importantly, the same survey also found majority of respondents in London ranked nature-based solutions of green infrastructure as their top priority of action during very hot weather, with 84% recognised green spaces as providing potential cooling benefits (Hewlett et al., 2026). Given that, London’s urban heat problem is not only defined by where heat concentrates, but also by whether heat exposed and socially deprived neighbourhoods can realistically access spaces for thermal relief. 2.1.2 Global and Local Policies Policies at both global and local scales have increasingly recognised urban heat as an equity and access problem. The United Nations (2023) emphasised the importance of making cities “inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable” through the Sustainable Development Goal 11. While not specifically foregrounded within the SDGs, the UNEP’s Beating the Heat: A Sustainable Cooling Handbook For Cities identifies community-centric cooling as a way “to advance social equity and environmental justice” and emphasises that cooling benefits should be reachable by marginalised communities, with priority for “those with the highest need first” (UNEP, 2021, pp. 150, 151). However, the effectiveness of these global initiatives depends on whether they are translated into local policy and planning actions. Existing urban heat-related policies have often focused on short-term management, including heat warning alerts, promoting behaviour change, and emergency service preparations (Norton et al., 2015). While these measures are important for reducing immediate heat risks, they do not fully address the structural and spatial causes of urban heat exposure. This also raises a temporal challenge, where policy response often lags accelerating climate risks. In the UK, the Climate Change Committee (2026) argues that “adaptation action is not keeping pace with increasing level of risk”. This also applies to England, where heat-related policies remain limited by insufficient understanding of who is vulnerable to extreme heat, how vulnerability varies spatially, and where neighbourhood-scale interventions should be targeted (Howarth et al., 2023). This is also the case for London. The city demonstrates growing interest in mitigating heat risk as well as recognising the role of green infrastructure in responding to urban heat risk and environmental inequalities. This is evident through the London Plan 2021 (Mayor of London, 2021), setting out a spatial development strategy encompassing heat risk, green infrastructure and open space accessibility. Further policy frameworks and tools include the London Green Infrastructure Framework (Mayor of London, 2026c), heat risk mapping in the London Climate Risk Map (Mayor of London, 2024b), Cool Spaces Map (Mayor of London, 2024a) and Heat Ready London (Mayor of London, 2026b). Nevertheless, despite policy ambitions, London’s approach remains limited and fragmented (see Section 5.3), particularly in terms of linking cooling benefits of green infrastructure with accessibility during heat (Turcu, 2025). Furthermore, while strategic policies are often set at the municipal level, implementation relies on borough and local-level planning as well as cross-borough and cross-sector coordination. Given this implementation gap, this shows a need for London’s urban heat-related policy to move beyond recognition of green infrastructure and towards neighbourhood-scale evidence on whether cooling-effective spaces are accessible for heat-vulnerable communities. 2.2 Cooling Benefits of Urban Green Space As discussed, studies and policies have emphasised UGS as an integrated climate adaptation strategy to counteract UHI effects and heat injustice. Increasingly positioned as a nature-based cooling infrastructure, UGS is widely recognised for its ability to regulate local thermal conditions and provision of public spaces for thermal relief (Bowler et al., 2010b; Norton et al., 2015). Vegetation has been proven to considerably intercept solar radiation and reduce heat absorbed and retained by land surfaces through shading, evapotranspiration, transpiration and thermal insulation (Bowler et al., 2010b; Kumar et al., 2024). For instance, parks are on average found to be 0.94 °C cooler, while specifically a study in London found an average cooling effect of 1.1°C and can reach up to 4°C at night time (Bowler et al., 2010b; Doick, Peace and Hutchings, 2014). Given this, UGS forms the park cool island effect, which creates cooler microclimatic conditions within green spaces than in adjacent built-up environments (Bowler et al., 2010b; Ren et al., 2013), providing higher levels of thermal comfort within otherwise heat-exposed urban environments (Aram et al., 2019; Balany et al., 2020). However, the cooling effects of UGS are not uniform and do not provide equal levels of thermal relief. The extent of UGS’s cooling benefits depends on size, spatial configuration of the greenspace, also the form and structure of the surrounding urban environment, and the prevailing meteorological patterns (Doick, Peace and Hutchings, 2014; L. Li et al., 2025; Wang and Ren, 2025). Size is often identified as a key factor in cooling performance, as larger UGS is often associated with more significant cooling effects from a more diverse and extensive vegetation cover, providing greater cooling intensity and distance compared to smaller UGS (Aram et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2021). However, this should not be interpreted as “bigger is better” in cooling means. For instance, Peng et al. (2021) identified diminishing cooling returns beyond very large sized parks in Shenzhen, with an upper threshold of 429ha while Wang et al. (2025) suggested a much smaller optimal park area upper limit of 56ha in Hangzhou, where an increase in size will not significantly enhance the cooling effects. At the other end of the size scale, some studies suggest that pocket parks below 2ha may be too small to generate substantial cooling effects, whereas others shows that those as small as 0.2ha, can still contribute to a cooling of around 0.3 °C (Vaz Monteiro et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2025). Additionally, spatial configuration also influences the magnitude and spatial extent of UGS cooling performance. Existing research commonly uses indicators of “cooling intensity” and “maximum cooling distance” to quantify cooling-effectiveness under different contexts, with cooling intensity measuring the temperature difference between the UGS and its surrounding environment and cooling distance measuring how far this cooling effect can extend (Wang et al., 2025). While compact green spaces are often found associated with stronger cooling intensity, irregular, fragmented and more complex shapes may extend cooling effects over longer distances through greater contact with the surrounding urban landscape (Feyisa, Dons and Meilby, 2014; Peng et al., 2021; L. Li et al., 2025). However, a study in London suggests that such greater edge effects may also come at the expense of lower cooling intensity, as higher complexity and perimeter/ area ratios may provide weaker internal cooling effects (Vaz Monteiro et al., 2016). These findings suggest that there is no “optimal” green space composition and configuration, as different spatial forms may influence the extent of cooling benefits differently (Peng et al., 2021). For this reason, park cooling intensity (PCI) indicators are often used to quantify the cooling effects of green spaces (Wu et al., 2025). Given this, whether UGS provides meaningful cooling benefits should be assessed spatially, considering the spatial continuity of cooling effects with increasing distance from UGS (Peng et al., 2021). In this sense, UGS should not be understood as a homogeneous form of cooling infrastructure, as UGS provision does not directly mean cooling-effectiveness. Therefore, it is necessary to identify and distinguish green spaces that demonstrate measurable cooling benefits as cooling infrastructure. 2.3 Equitable Access to Cooling Infrastructure Building on Section 2.2, in the context of urban heat, cooling benefits of UGS should not be evaluated only by their potential cooling performance, but also whether they are accessible. Accessibility here refers to the availability and “ease” of reaching UGS and its provided qualities by “overcoming spatial barriers” of distance, time and cost associated with access to diverse means of transport modes (Liu, Kwan and Kan, 2021; Huang et al., 2023; Czesak and Różycka-Czas, 2025). Existing studies often measure UGS accessibility through proximity and threshold-based approaches, such as static Euclidean distance, distance decay approaches, buffer-based standards of 300-500m, and increasingly the 15-minute city concept (Kabisch et al., 2016; Jalkanen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023; Almeida and Fonseca, 2025; Czesak and Różycka-Czas, 2025). Similar standards are applied in the UK, where the Accessible Greenspace Standard recognises local accessibility as having access to at least 2ha of greenspace within 300m from home (Natural England, 2026a). Although these measures and policy tools provide simple, comparable and policy relevant benchmarks, they remain limited as accessibility is multidimensional, primarily considering proximity may overlook other features such as quality (Rigolon et al., 2018). While quality often refers to amenities, maintenance and safety across literature, cooling-effectiveness represents a functional quality of UGS that is essential for these benefits to be realised under urban heat contexts (Rigolon et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2023). Accessibility should therefore not only be understood as the spatial presence of UGS within a given distance, but as realistic access to cooling-effective UGS as cooling infrastructure. Given the complexity of real-world travel patterns, accessibility to UGS is also shaped by transport system attributes, temporal variability and individual spatiotemporal constraints (Nie et al., 2024; Schendl et al., 2025). Infrastructure-based metrics are often used to provide a more comprehensive indication of how individuals practically move through cities, incorporating distance to public transport stops, travel times, network connectivity and service levels (Nie et al., 2024). Additionally, it is widely acknowledged that individuals experience different levels of accessibility, as they may adopt different travel modes (i.e. walking, cycling and public transit (PT)) even when travelling to the same destinations, depending on the relationship between distance, travel time and willingness to travel (Chen et al., 2022). For instance, studies show that individuals often use public transport to access larger UGS, and that frequently visited UGS may be located well beyond commonly assumed travel-distance thresholds (Czesak and Różycka-Czas, 2025; Hassan et al., 2025). This is particularly relevant in large cities with dense public transport and pedestrian infrastructure like London, where simple thresholds can be misleading as urban centres may benefit more from short-distance access, while outer areas depend more on rail networks (Duan, Chen and Roosli, 2026). Travel-time based measures are therefore considered more realistic and appropriate as they account for transport mode, network structure and temporal variation by time of day and day of the week (Miller, 2018). Given this, evaluating accessibility under multimodal transportation can capture heterogeneous accessibility patterns, enabling mode- and location-specific disparities to cooling-effective UGS to be identified and examined across neighbourhoods. Ensuring adequate and equitable access to cooling infrastructure has become an increasing EJ concern in the context of urban heat and as a critical aspect of sustainable development (Xu et al., 2022; Dong et al., 2024). By definition, EJ refers to the unequal exposure to environmental burdens and the unequal access to environmental goods experienced by different socioeconomic and ethnic groups, particularly on UGS (Rigolon, 2016; Kronenberg et al., 2020). As discussed in Section 2.1.2, UGS is often promoted as an urban heat mitigation strategy with institutional frameworks emphasising inclusivity and equity. Nevertheless, scholars documented cooling-effective UGS as a “luxury good” in reality, whereby such spaces are unevenly distributed, disproportionately concentrated in wealthier areas and less accessible from lower-income neighbourhoods (Y. Li et al., 2024; Ngan et al., 2025). On the other hand, this does not always systematically disadvantage lower socioeconomic groups, nor consistently favour those advantaged socioeconomic groups, as patterns of spatial equity vary by specific urban context and are sensitive to how accessibility is measured (Lu et al., 2024). Therefore, evaluating access should also consider the needs of different population groups (Williams et al., 2020). Building on Dong et al. (2024) and Williams et al. (2020), areas with higher heat risk or more vulnerable residents can be understood as having higher cooling needs, as they in many cases need and have most to gain from the benefits of cooling infrastructures. For this reason, this study extends the concept of EJ into a cooling justice problem, whereby inequalities are shaped by the interaction between heat exposure, physiological, social vulnerability (Section 2.1), and accessibility (Section 2.3) to cooling-effective UGS (Section 2.2). Specifically, these are examined through heat exposure and socioeconomic deprivation. 2.4 Measuring Cooling Accessibility and Spatial Equity Having established access to cooling-effective UGS as a cooling justice concern in the previous sections, the following will review existing methodological approaches and inform methodology choices for this study. Existing literature employs a diverse approach to evaluate the UHI and cooling effect, using air temperature (Doick, Peace and Hutchings, 2014), LST (Xu et al., 2022; Krenz and Amann, 2025) or both (Du et al., 2024). Air temperature from in-situ measurements (i.e. data loggers,measurements from meteorological stations) is often considered to be a more representative measure of human thermal exposure (Doick, Peace and Hutchings, 2014; Y. Li et al., 2025). However, its spatial coverage is often limited by sparse distribution of measuring stations, resulting in low spatial resolution (Sobrino et al., 2012; Y. Li et al., 2025). Alternatively, thermal infrared remote sensing (RS) imagery is widely used to retrieve LST (Du et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023), providing spatially continuous measurements, suitable for city-scale analysis (Weng, 2009; Yang, Yan and Zhang, 2020; Li et al., 2023). Earlier studies relied on LST measurements by AVHRR and MODIS satellite sensors, recent research has increasingly used higher resolution ASTER (90m) and Landsat (30m) for capturing finer LST spatial variations (Imran et al., 2022). Nevertheless, satellite-derived LST is influenced by the sensor’s resolution, and may overestimate cooling benefits relative to ground level air temperature (Sobrino et al., 2012; Du et al., 2024). However, given the statistically significant relationship between LST and air temperature, LST is supported as a spatially comprehensive approach for identifying urban surface heating patterns at city-scale (Yang, Yan and Zhang, 2020; Krenz and Amann, 2025). Moving on to cooling accessibility, simple distance-based measures may oversimplify true representations of urban mobilities. Given this, travel-time inputs estimated by assigning average travel speeds to road segments may not fully account for differences in routing between travel modes, potentially resulting in deviations in accessibility estimates (Chen et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023). Advancing on this, studies attempted to use network-based approaches to improve the reliability of travel-time estimation through scheduled timetable feed data using a General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format (Pereira, Andrade and Vieira, 2023). GTFS provides detailed information on routes, timetables and stops, enabling more granular and scalable analyses for public transit accessibility (Pereira, Andrade and Vieira, 2023; Lee and van Dijk, 2026). To integrate GTFS data with road networks, open-source routing tools such as r5r have emerged as more transparent and reproducible alternatives to proprietary routing methods, enabling efficient multimodal computation of many-to-many pairs of origin-destination queries (Pereira et al., 2021). While previous studies have applied r5r to broader accessibility analysis, including public transport accessibility in the UK (Verduzco Torres and McArthur, 2024), spatial equity in job accessibility in London (Lee and van Dijk, 2026) and UGS accessibility across European cities (Wozniak, Radzimski and Wajchman-Świtalska, 2025), its applications to UGS with demonstrated cooling benefits remain limited. Further, accessibility can be assessed over a variety of measures, including infrastructure-, location-, person- and utility-based measures (Geurs and van Wee, 2004; Miller, 2018). As “there is no objective, normative standard for what constitutes ‘good’ or ‘acceptable’ accessibility” (Miller, 2018, p. 553), measure selection should be tailored to the specific study purpose. For assessing cooling-effective UGS accessibility, location-based approaches are considered appropriate. Across accessibility literature, inequalities have been commonly examined through descriptive, correlational, and mapping approaches, with regression frequently used to assess relationships between accessibility and socioeconomic or spatial factors (Hidayati, Tan and Yamu, 2021). While ordinary least squares (OLS) modelling has been applied to green space and cooling UGS accessibility equity studies (Wu et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2022), it is considered less suitable for this study given the count nature of cumulative opportunity measures and potential spatial dependence between neighbouring areas. Considering this, Bayesian hierarchical models (BHM) provide an alternative approach. Despite being widely used in disease mapping (Gause et al., 2024), BHM have also been applied to housing, health and well-being (Kandt et al., 2017) and UGS and health inequalities research (Liu et al., 2026), demonstrating their potential in examining spatial inequalities across urban contexts. Yet, global modelling approaches may hide spatially concentrated inequalities, which is crucial for identifying priority locations that could benefit from EJ-related interventions. Given this, local indicators of spatial association (LISA) can further identify any localised spatial mismatches. Studies also utilise a bivariate measure of LISA, so-called BiLISA, to further unveil mismatches between two geographical variables (Wang, Ouyang and Zhang, 2024). In this vein, this methodology allows moving beyond interpreting accessibility patterns to examining whether neighbourhoods with relatively greater needs systematically experience differentiated levels of cooling access. Altogether, prior literature established urban heat as an uneven socio-spatial problem and UGS as a potential mitigation resource, less attention has been paid to whether UGS that provide measurable cooling are reachable by neighbourhoods with the greatest needs. To the best of our knowledge, no research in London has integrated UGS cooling performance, accessibility and heat vulnerability within one framework. Addressing this gap, this study integrates Earth observations, cooling effect assessments, travel-time accessibility and equity analyses to examine the extent to which heat exposed, and socioeconomically deprived neighbourhoods have equitable access to cooling-effective UGS. Adopting a vertical equity approach, greater equity is assumed when cooling-effective UGS opportunities increase with heat exposure and socioeconomic deprived neighbourhoods (Khanyile and Fatti, 2022). Likewise, low accessibility in areas of relatively higher need is therefore interpreted to be an EJ mismatch. Using London as a case study, the following sections provide neighbourhood-scale evidence to inform more targeted urban heat adaptation, supporting the city’s transition to becoming “heat ready”.

This section will outline the methodological approach for this study, following the study’s objectives to identify cooling-effective UGS and heat exposure across neighbourhoods (3.4), assess spatial distribution and multimodal accessibility of cooling-effective UGS as cooling opportunities (3.5), and examine accessibility equity across neighbourhoods in relation to patterns of heat exposure and socioeconomic deprivation (3.6). 3.1 Statement of Ethics All data sources are secondary and are publicly available and accessible. Neither primary data collection nor individuals will be involved or identifiable in the analysis or outputs. This study recognises ethnicity data derived from Census 2021 as sociopolitical constructs rather than biologically founded categories when classifying ethnic minority groups. Also acknowledging the ecological fallacy, where neighbourhood-level findings from aggregated data should not be assumed to represent the characteristics and experiences of individuals residing in the studied areas (Firebaugh, 2001). Therefore, results are presented carefully, with clear acknowledgement of methods, assumptions and limitations in the following sections. Accordingly, this study is considered minimal risk and exempt from ethical approval. All sources are cited transparently and in accordance with any specified access conditions. The analysis was carried out using Google Earth Engine (GEE) and R (version 4.5.2). The main R-packages used in this study are enclosed in Table E1. Regarding reproducibility, the code used to conduct this analysis is available in this GitHub repository, including all figures presented in this study. 3.2 Study Area This study focuses on Greater London, the capital of the United Kingdom (Figure 1). London has an expansive area of approximately 1,572 square kilometres, with a total population of 9,089,736 in 2024 (Office for National Statistics, n.d.a). It exhibits a spatially heterogeneous urban structure, with substantial variation in population density, demographics, employment, transportation connectivity, and socioeconomic diversity across both inner and outer London. Although around 20% of London is public green space, its provision is unevenly distributed, with access varying considerably across different neighbourhoods. This study therefore assesses UGS accessibility at Lower layer Super Output Areas (LSOA) level. LSOAs are small geographic statistical units, containing a residential population of approximately 1,000 to 3,000 each, with 4,994 LSOAs across London. UGS ≥ 2ha were included in this study as candidate sites, given their potential cooling capacity to serve as meaningful resources for communities (Almeida and Fonseca, 2025). The resulting intra-urban SUHII indicates the relative thermal deviation of each neighbourhood from the London mean. The formula as follows (MacLachlan et al., 2017; Hoffman, Shandas and Pendleton, 2020): \[\begin{equation} \mathrm{SUHII}_{i} = \overline{\mathrm{LST}}_{i} - \overline{\mathrm{LST}}_{\mathrm{other}} \tag{3.2} \end{equation}\] 3.4.2 Park Cooling Effect Cooling effects were assessed for 1,837 UGS ≥ 2ha1, following the exclusion of 31 non-polygon features (i.e. LineString and Points). Given that cooling effect is non-linear with distance and varies by different functions and conditions, cooling-effectiveness of UGS was assessed from an accumulative perspective using PCI and park cooling gradient (PCG) to account for spatial continuity (Peng et al., 2021). Considering the 30m spatial resolution of Landsat imagery and previous evidence that cooling distance limits within 900m from the UGS boundary (Peng et al., 2021; Du et al., 2022), thirty 30m wide buffers zones were created offset from each UGS boundary to quantify the spatial extent and magnitude of park cooling effects (see Figure 4). The first turning point (first local maximum) within 30-900 meters from the UGS boundary was identified as maximum cooling distance (L), with the fitted temperature at this turning point as the surrounding LST (\(T_{L}\)) where cooling influence from UGS diminishes beyond this point. As identified by the fitted curve (illustrated in Figure 5), the maximum cooling distance (\(L\)) and its corresponding LST (\(T_{L}\)) will be used to calculate PCI and PCG. PCI is defined as the ratio of accumulated LST reduction within the maximum cooling distance, with higher PCI values demonstrating better cooling effect (Peng et al., 2021; Du et al., 2022; Xiong, Xie and Yang, 2024) PCG was calculated as the accumulated LST reduction by maximum cooling distance, with higher PCG values indicating stronger heat absorption capacities (Peng et al., 2021; Xiong, Xie and Yang, 2024). Both formulas are as follows: \[\begin{equation} \mathrm{PCI} = \frac{L \times T_L - \int_{0}^{L} T(r)\,dr} {L \times T_L} \tag{3.4} \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \mathrm{PCG} = \frac{L \times T_L - \int_{0}^{L} T(r)\,dr} {L} \tag{3.5} \end{equation}\] where, \(L\) = Maximum cooling distance \(T_{L}\) = LST at maximum cooling distance \(L\times T_{L}\) = Cumulative fitted LST within distance L \(\int_{0}^{L} T(r)\,dr\) = Cumulative sum of the LST at each distance from the UGS boundary \(L \times T_L - \int_{0}^{L} T(r)\,dr\) = Cooling LST of the UGS. The following were considered for the identification of cooling-effective UGS, where UGS not meeting these criteria in reducing surrounding temperatures were excluded: Valid cooling distance: maximum cooling distance (\(L\)) situated within 30-900 meters; Maximum temperature reduction: the LST difference between LST at the maximum cooling distance (\(T_{L}\)) and the internal LST of UGS >0; PCI: accumulated LST reduction within (\(L\)) as a ratio >0; PCG: accumulated LST reduction divided by (\(L\)) >0. Further considering for publicly accessible cooling-effective UGS, functions identified as Public Park or Garden and Playing Field are selected following the Accessible Greenspace Assessment (Natural England, 2026b). Other functions2 are not considered, as they are in many cases not publicly accessible, are not actual greenspaces or require paid access (Natural England, 2026b; Smith et al., 2026b). Given the count nature of our dependent variables, OLS regression is not appropriate for this study. Instead, two types of count variable regressions of negative binomial and Poisson regression were considered. While both likelihoods allow zero values, negative binomial likelihoods can further handle overdispersed data (when variance exceeds mean). Given this, both were fitted with the same set of variables for each outcome. They are then compared with their corresponding Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) values, where models indicating better goodness-of-fit with lower AICs were selected as the distributional family for modelling (see Table B1) (Coxe, West and Aiken, 2009). Subsequently, global Moran’s I5 was used to check for spatial autocorrelation of GLM residuals to identify any spatial relationships of unobserved patterns (see Table B2). Due to presence of strong positive spatial autocorrelation in Moran’s I results, next, BHM using Besag-York-Mollié (BYM2)6 spatial specifications are implemented with integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA)7 through the R-INLA8 package to account for spatial dependence. Likewise, negative binomial and Poisson BYM2 models were fitted for each outcome, with likelihoods selected based on model comparison by reported Deviance Information Criteria (DIC), Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC), Conditional Predictive Ordinate (CPO) and marginal likelihood (MLIK) values (Branion-Calles et al., 2026; Ngutuka et al., 2026) (see Table B3). The regression is formulated for each of the 6 dependent variables of the accessibility in a specific LSOA (i) across PT, walking and cycling travel modes with specified time thresholds. Model equation is as follows, with b_{i} denotes spatially structured and unstructured effects based on an adjacency graph constructed by Queen contiguity: \[\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \log(\mu_i) =\;& \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathrm{IMD}_i + \beta_2 \mathrm{SUHII}_i + \beta_3 (\mathrm{IMD}_i \times \mathrm{SUHII}_i) \\ &+ \beta_4 \mathrm{Age}_{0\text{--}4,i} + \beta_5 \mathrm{Age}_{65+,i} + \beta_6 \mathrm{EthnicMinority}_i \\ &+ \beta_7 \mathrm{PopulationDensity}_i + \beta_8 \mathrm{InnerOuterLondon}_i + b_i \end{aligned} \tag{3.8} \end{equation}\] As the linear predictor is defined on the logarithm scale, model results are interpreted by exponentiating the posterior mean coefficient \((e^{\beta })\) to obtain the incidence rate ratio (IRR), with the exponentiated 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles reported as 95% posterior credible intervals (CI) (Astell-Burt et al., 2014; Branion-Calles et al., 2026). Here, IRR of 1 indicates no associations, where above 1 indicates positive and below 1 indicates negative associations per one unit change in the standard deviation for standardised continuous variables (Astell-Burt et al., 2014). Following, BYM2 model residuals’ spatial variation was examined by Moran’s I for any remaining spatial autocorrelation. To further identify local spatial associations in accessibility equity, BiLISA was performed using the spdep package for cross-variable examination between accessibility indicators (observed variables) and the key equity indicators of heat exposure and socioeconomic deprivation (spatially lagged variables) across neighbourhoods. Resulting statistics classified as High-High, High-Low, Low-Low, Low-High (L-H) or not significant (Ermagun, Janatabadi and Maharjan, 2023) will be interpreted according to the definition of equity established in Section 2.4. L-H clustering will be interpreted as areas with patterns of inequity and relatively equitable conditions indicating High-Low. SUHII was positively associated with cooling-effective UGS accessibility across all models, with IRRs ranging from 1.010 to 1.084 (95%CI excluding 1). Posterior evidence indicates that a one-standard-deviation increase in SUHII was associated with higher access to cooling-effective UGS with other variables held constant. Notably, the associations were stronger under 15-minute (4.1-8.4%) compared to 60-minute models (1.0-1.8%). In contrast, IMD showed limited posterior support across most models featuring credible intervals that included 1, of which only Model 4 indicated evidence for a negative association with accessibility (IRR=0.9888, 95%CI=0.979-0.998). Further, the interaction between SUHII and IMD was negative across all models and found credible in all three 15-minute threshold models (Model 1, 3 and 5) and the 60-minute model by cycling (Model 6). Overall, this indicates that positive associations between accessibility and heat exposure tended to weaken upon the influence of higher neighbourhood deprivation. Following the inclusion of spatial effects in BYM2 models, residual Moran’s I values were substantially reduced in comparison to GLM models, although some indication of spatial autocorrelation remains (see Table C2). Despite improvements in accounting for spatial dependence, the observed adjusted PIT distributions were generally bell-shaped (Figure C1), indicating some remaining predictive overdispersion and miscalibration across models. BiLISA clustering analysis identified statistically significant (p-value < 0.05) local clusters of low accessibility surrounded by high heat exposure and/or deprivation (see Table D1). Zooming into L-H clusters, these accounted for 7.0-12.0% of LSOAs across 15- and 60-minute specifications. This is further examined through mapping approaches (Figure 13, Figure 14), which display overlapping heat exposure and/or deprivation L-H clusters spatially. Across all modes and travel time thresholds, L-H clusters were generally concentrated in north-east and eastern London, with several clusters along the western and northern periphery. Under the 15-minute threshold, clusters were more spatially dispersed across north-eastern, western and inner London. Conversely, these spatial clusters were more concentrated under the 60-minute threshold in north-east and eastern parts of the city. Observable differences between heat exposure and IMD patterns also indicate that neighbourhoods experiencing relatively greater heat exposure were not necessarily those experiencing greater deprivation. Chapter 5 Discussion Building on the results as established in Section 4, this section will evaluate the key findings (5.1 and 5.2) and implications of these results in the context of green infrastructure and urban heat planning (5.3) in response to our research question of to what extent is multimodal accessibility to cooling-effective UGS equitably distributed across heat exposed and socioeconomically deprived areas in London? Following, this section will also discuss transferability (5.4), limitations (5.5) and outline directions for future research (5.6) for this study. 5.1 Availability of Cooling-Effective Urban Green Space and Accessibility Given the spatial disparities in surface heat exposure across London (Figure 9), the findings highlighted the potential role of UGS as cooling infrastructure, consistent with prior evidence (Norton et al., 2015). Although previous literature suggests that higher UGS coverage and fragmented spatial configurations can influence cooling performance and green space connectivity (Wang and Ren, 2025), such measures may overlook whether UGS demonstrate effective cooling and are publicly accessible. This is evident in the case of London, where cooling performances varied substantially between UGS, with only approximately one third (32.77%) of the UGS studied were identified as both cooling-effective and publicly accessible (Figure 10) as cooling infrastructure (defined in Section 2.2 and 2.3). In good agreement with previous studies (Xu et al., 2022), having a large supply of UGS distributed across London may not translate into having an equally extensive network of UGS as cooling infrastructure. Despite Outer London’s wider provision of green infrastructure through the metropolitan Green Belt (Weihermüller and Doyle, 2026), this does not necessarily translate into reduced travel time to, or having more accessible opportunities for cooling-effective UGS for these surrounding neighbourhoods. This may reflect the geography of Outer London, which is generally characterised by weaker transport infrastructure and higher levels of car dependency (Lee and van Dijk, 2026). Moreover, the observed spatial patterns may also reflect London’s historical urban development, whereby earlier industrialisation contributed to a compact urban structure with higher density of population and transport provision within urban centres (Duan, Chen and Roosli, 2026). As established in literature review, existing green space accessibility policy standards and studies often favour proximity and walking-based measures (Kabisch et al., 2016; Natural England, 2026a). However, as pointed by Geurs and van Wee (2004, p. 137), “interpretation can be much improved by estimating the separate influence of the different components of accessibility”. Acknowledging network-based travel time across different transport modes, our results demonstrated that modal disparities also shaped differentiated cooling-effective UGS opportunities across neighbourhoods in London, generally consistent with previous studies (S. Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). We found that cycling provided stronger local accessibility within 15 minutes, whereas PT enabled access to a substantially wider scope of opportunities reachable within 60 minutes. This highlights that beyond UGS provision, the relative accessibility of neighbourhoods varies depending on how accessibility is measured. In the context of London, simple “closeness” and a focus on walking access may therefore neglect actual travel conditions and oversimplify how the transport network shapes cooling-effective UGS access in reality. Nevertheless, these findings indicate potential accessibility, as real-world accessibility also depends on one’s need, ability, and willingness to travel. 5.2 Spatial Equity in Cooling-Effective Urban Green Space Accessibility The findings from BYM2 models showed limited evidence of consistent independent relationships between socioeconomic deprivation and poorer cooling-effective UGS accessibility across most models. Although this contrasts with common theories of environmental and distributional injustice in previous research, which often conceptualise disadvantaged populations as having lower UGS access (Boone and Klinsky, 2015), it is compatible with other studies where socioeconomic inequalities can be inconsistent (Rigolon, 2016). In the UK context, one possible explanation may relate to the historical legacy of UGS distribution, where earlier placements of working-class neighbourhoods near UGS as a public health measure may have contributed to differentiated access in certain deprived neighbourhoods to date (Mears et al., 2019). Notably, our results indicate higher heat exposure was associated with higher accessibility across models. This can partly be explained by London’s urban structure, whereby denser urban areas may retain greater heat while also providing greater connectivity to wider cooling opportunities. Meanwhile, socioeconomic deprivation appears to modify the relationship between higher heat exposure and accessibility. As established in Section 2.3, cooling justice advocates for equitable access in relation to heat exposure and socioeconomic deprivation. From a distributional EJ perspective, London’s evidence showed some misalignment between cooling-effective UGS accessibility and environmental and socioeconomic needs, broadly consistent with the mixed demand-oriented equity findings across international evidence (Tian et al., 2024). This therefore uncovers relative disadvantage for socioeconomically deprived neighbourhoods but does not illustrate an overall distinct pattern of inequality across London. Our BiLISA spatial clustering analysis usefully complemented the BYM2 models, revealing the spatial heterogeneity at the local level, agreeing that inequity “is more evident at smaller spatial scales” (Hu et al., 2020, p. 7). Looking into the L-H clusters, our findings highlighted spatial mismatch with neighbourhoods with poorer cooling-effective UGS access and surrounding higher heat exposure or higher socioeconomic deprivation as a relative inequity condition to be concerned for. Such patterns indicated that access to cooling opportunities does not necessarily correspond with areas of relatively greater need in the case of London, broadly similar to earlier findings by Wang, Ouyang and Zhang (2024). These L-H clusters also coincide in certain neighbourhoods (see Figure 13, Figure 14), showing neighbourhoods with compounded cooling justice concerns. These disparities may reflect London’s land use pressures, where conventional green-space planning tends to be constrained by a trade-off between protecting and enhancing UGS while addressing affordable housing needs (Whitten, 2022). Such densification may exacerbate urban heat through increased impervious surface cover, thereby intensifying existing cooling inequities (Norton et al., 2015). From the cooling justice perspective, identifying these potential spatial mismatches as priority “hotspots” allows more targeted local interventions according to relative community needs. Regardless, the L-H clusters persist and vary across modes and under different travel time thresholds. This adds on our discussion in Section 5.1, that examining through a single-mode measure may not provide a comprehensive picture of cooling-effective UGS accessibility inequity, as people from different socioeconomic groups may adopt different travel behaviours and mode choices (Hu et al., 2020). Taking everything into account, cooling-effective UGS accessibility does not show a global equity pattern but instead persists through localised spatial mismatches. As such, these findings highlight key areas of prioritisation, of which their implications will be further discussed in Section 5.3. 5.3 Implications for Urban Heat Policy The L-H clusters presented and discussed in Section 4.3 and 5.2 warrant attention, pointing to where green infrastructure interventions could be prioritised and targeted alongside broader green infrastructure network planning across London. Notably, several boroughs in London would benefit from priority policy interventions, namely areas within Hillingdon, Ealing, Hounslow, Enfield, Haringey, Havering and Barking and Dagenham, where L-H clusters were persistent across travel modes and time thresholds. This aligns with the recent publication of Heat Ready London, which stresses the need to “reduce inequalities by prioritising those most at risk … impacted by heat” and “with the least access to green space” as key objectives for achieving a heat-resilient London (Mayor of London, 2026b, pp. 9–10, 21). Further, the recently released Draft London Plan 2026 demonstrates growing attention to urban heat within London’s planning agenda. While the London Plan 2021 recognises the need to manage heat risk (SI4), the current draft shows growing policy emphasis on heat risk (GHR4) and improving access to green space (GHR8), particularly in areas of deficiency (AoD) and local green infrastructure priorities (Mayor of London, 2026a). While AoD provides a useful policy benchmark, its proximity-based nature may overlook differences in access across modes. Based on our neighbourhood-level multimodal accessibility findings discussed previously, this provides complementary insights into where and through which transport modes access to existing cooling opportunities is relatively limited, allowing more targeted accessibility improvements to existing provision. As acquiring new UGS is complicated and expensive (Rigolon, 2016), improving access to existing cooling infrastructure may offer a more achievable short-term approach for London for reducing current accessibility gaps. Furthermore, given that the Draft London Plan is currently under public consultation, such evidence could also contribute to identifying areas of local green infrastructure accessibility deficiencies and inform heat-resilience interventions. Beyond the shortlisted areas of priority intervention, improving awareness of the availability and accessibility of these cooling opportunities is crucial, given EJ is also a “fairness in process” (Boone and Klinsky, 2015, p. 330). London’s current policy tool, the Cool Space Map recognises indoor and outdoor spaces for heat mitigation during hot weather, yet limits outdoor cooling opportunities features to tree canopy cover and vaguely “cooler area” only (Mayor of London, 2024a). Following our identification of cooling-effective UGS across London in Section 5.1, such evidence could be integrated into existing policy mapping tools to further promote outdoor cooling opportunities and reinforce the role of UGS to facilitate as cooling infrastructure for heat mitigation. More importantly, to realise the full potential of UGS as cooling infrastructure also depends on managing and maintaining their capacity for the long-term. Following recent drought conditions and wildfire events across London, this highlighted the vulnerability of green spaces under prolonged periods of extreme heat. It is therefore important to ensure the quality and safety of these spaces alongside appropriate vegetation management to sustain their cooling benefits and ensure usability during high temperatures. 5.4 Transferability While previous sections discussed the implications for the case of London, the reproducible methodological framework implemented in this study could also be applied to other metropolitan regions in the UK (e.g. Greater Manchester) or globally. Even so, the full replicability is subject to data availability in the selected study context, and accessibility modelling parameters and thresholds may require adjustments according to the specific urban context. More importantly, London-specific findings should not be directly extrapolated to other contexts with different urban structure and sociodemographic geographies, as such variations may shape how the outcomes should be understood. 5.5 Limitations Several data and methodological limitations that may influence the temporal and spatial interpretation of our findings is recognised. Firstly, there is a temporal mismatch across datasets (2021-2026) due to data availability. Covering only one summer period, our findings therefore represent a cross-sectional assessment encompassing different time periods, where LST variations between years or extreme heat events fall beyond the study scope. Methodologically, while excluding UGS < 2ha is informed by wider literature and policy benchmarks, this may potentially overlook the cooling benefits of smaller UGS (i.e. pocket parks), particularly in urban centres where smaller UGS contribute to a substantial proportion of local UGS provision. Additionally, disturbances such as vegetation, water bodies and large impervious surfaces within buffer rings were not removed. The calculated mean LST of surrounding areas may reflect influences of the wider environmental context on top of the cooling effect of the UGS. It is also worth noting that satellite-derived LST represents surface thermal conditions (as discussed in Section 2.4). Accordingly, the identified cooling effects should be interpreted as surface cooling, not a direct representation human thermal comfort. This study also recognises the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP), whereby aggregating data under different spatial scales can provide inconsistent results (Wong, 2009). Using LSOA as spatial units for analyses although is considered a practical choice here, it may compromise interpretation of data, introduce statistical bias and overlook accessibility variations within certain neighbourhoods. As our BYM2 spatial effects were defined by LSOA-level Queen contiguity spatial weights, the remaining residuals spatial autocorrelation and predictive miscalibration in our models may partially reflect sensitivity to the specified spatial structure. Nevertheless, the models still provided inferential conclusions regarding the observed associations. Despite the shortcomings, our findings provide a preliminary neighbourhood-scale assessment of equity in potential accessibility to cooling-effective UGS across London, highlighting new avenues for future research and applications. 5.6 Future Direction Following Section 5.5, future directions could extend on these three areas. 1) Future research can expand on the temporal scope across longer periods and/or multiple seasons for a more comprehensive understanding of the temporal stability of UGS cooling performances and spatial mismatches. 2) Further accounting for UGS capacity, quality (e.g. attractiveness, safety), and population perceptions can complement objective accessibility measures, allowing a more comprehensive assessment of cooling justice. Improving reachable opportunities is important, yet they may overlook how UGS are perceived or used by local communities, as residents in some cases “do not see the greenspaces as provided for them” (Jones, Hillsdon and Coombes, 2009, p. 5). 3) Moving beyond the identified L-H clusters, further research can examine which urban environmental characteristics are associated with these mismatches at local levels, and identify context specific interventions for improving cooling accessibility (Zeng et al., 2026).

Chapter 6 Conclusion Under the increasing threat of urban heat, rising temperatures present a pressing challenge for many regions, calling for urgent and broad-based sustainable cooling solutions (UNEP, 2021). In this context, the role of urban green spaces (UGS) is beyond doubt critical in addressing urban heat and strengthening climate resilience, thereby ensuring fair access to cooling-effective UGS is essential. Otherwise, vulnerable populations may face greater impact, further exacerbating environmental justice (EJ). This study therefore examined how potential accessibility to cooling-effective UGS patterns was related to heat exposure and socioeconomic context in London. By integrating remote sensing (RS), network-based multimodal accessibility and spatial equity analysis, this offered a more comprehensive understanding of whether green spaces capable of providing measurable cooling benefits are also accessible to neighbourhoods with greater heat exposure and relative deprivation. The findings demonstrated substantial variation in both cooling performance and accessibility of UGS across London. Returning to our research question, the answer appears to be that multimodal accessibility to cooling-effective UGS is unevenly distributed across the city, with local inequities varying across heat exposed and socioeconomically deprived areas. Overall, these findings contribute to conventional green spaces accessibility and EJ research, demonstrating the importance of considering cooling performance, multi-mode accessibility and spatial patterns of areas of deficiency. Looking forward, addressing these spatial mismatches should involve more considerations towards equalising the benefits of cooling infrastructure and intervention strategies towards areas and communities most needed. Based on London’s evidence, we thus recommend to explicitly considering local cooling access within green infrastructure and heat resilience planning frameworks. With regard to future research, this approach provides a transferable and policy relevant starting point for further analyses. All in all, the implications contribute not only towards London’s long-term heat resilience but also supporting wider global initiatives for safe and accessible green spaces and climate adaptation, namely the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 11, 13 and the New Urban Agenda’s commitment for “well-connected and well-distributed networks of open, multipurpose, safe, inclusive, accessible and quality public spaces to improving the resilience of cities to disasters and climate change” (United Nations, 2015; UN Habitat, 2020, p. 19). Ultimately, the success of such policy ambitions in practice also requires collaboration between boroughs and stakeholders to turn spatial evidence into targeted and actionable solutions.
